verdict.conclusion: The D4 numbers reproduce exactly: 5.000 over 299-322 nm, 2.500 over 322.4-326.4 nm, 3.109 at 179.31 nm, 1.000 above 330 nm, identical across all five levels to <=1%.  But the D4 EXPLANATION is wrong: the deviation is not caused by the one-index wavelength misregistration between the two files (fixing that leaves the deviation intact) and is not a registration artefact in the sense proposed.  It is caused by a constant of 5.0 nm implicit in the optical calibration: the factor equals 5/(local wavelength sampling interval) to <=1% at 91% of points (median |deviation| 0.06%), i.e. the normalized series is per-bin (interval-weighted) while the grid flux is per-unit-wavelength, or vice versa.  The 'discrete' segments are exactly the pieces of the sampling ladder: 1 nm (299-321), 1.5 nm (321-322.5), 2 nm (322.5-326.5), 3.5 nm (326.5-330), 5 nm (>330), which is why the factor snaps to 5.0 / 2.5 and why it varies smoothly through the FUV where the interval grows smoothly.  The claim's inference that this is a data-product artefact rather than physics is CORRECT, and strongly confirmed: it is composition-blind to <=1% while the five compositions differ by up to 152x pointwise in the UV.

which_axis_carries_the_interval.note: both axes share the same sampling layout (1 nm band 299-321, 5 nm above 330), so this test cannot by itself say which file is per-bin and which is per-unit-wavelength; it only shows the interval is the right variable.

factor_ladder_summary.note: the two failing rungs (2.70 nm, 3.50 nm) contain the transition nodes 296.23 and 326.41 nm where the interval itself is ambiguous; every other rung matches 5/step

global_fit_with_vs_without_interval.note: the entire D4 deviation is removed by one factor, the local sampling interval, with no free parameter away from the optical calibration band
